gap: A gives the selection two identical 4px caret bars, one at each end (device runs x426–433 and x734–741, both 8×92px, both #00B5FF at 100% alpha) — nothing distinguishes anchor from focus, so the caret stops meaning "where I am" and there is no cue which edge shift+arrow will move. B at least differentiates its two ends (handle above-left vs below-right).
gapTheirs: B makes the selected word unreadable: the glyphs inside the selection drop to #4B8290 on a #003E4C fill — 2.7:1 contrast, versus A's #CCCCCC on #143E4F at 7.0:1 — and are struck through on top of that. Its selection handles are 44px device (22 CSS px) circles that bleed 21 CSS px above and below the 46px line box (top handle spans y950–1082 against a line box of y992–1083), sitting directly on the glyphs of the line above and below.
verdict: The light-mode carets are effectively the same object in both — 8–9 device px (4 CSS px) of flat #00B5FF spanning the full 92px line box, a bar twice the width a text caret should be and tall enough to overshoot the ascender, so neither wins there and both read as a block, not a hairline instrument. The dark selection decides it: B hangs 22px touch-style dots off both ends of the range, which collide with the lines above and below and turn a keyboard selection into a phone gesture, and then dims and strikes the selected word down to 2.7:1 so you cannot read the thing you are about to replace. A's version is dumber but honest — the word stays at 7:1, nothing overlaps the neighbouring lines, and the range edge is the same 4px bar as the caret. A's real sin is that the two edge bars are identical, so the caret loses its one job of telling you where the next keystroke lands.

builderNote: Rebuilt the caret from re-measured iA pixels: #00b5ff, 0.155 em wide snapped to whole CSS px, height = full line pitch, and the band anchored 68.75% above / 31.25% below a runtime-measured baseline (iA sits lower than a CSS line box, centred on the ink rather than the em box), with the left edge nudged 0.07 em past the advance cell so it lands where the next glyph's ink begins; it rests on left/top rather than a transform so both edges are hard device pixels. The selection now paints in a new #sel-layer *under* the ink — the native textarea selection painted over #mirror and veiled selected text from #1c1c1c to #153d4d — snapped to the same band as the caret, with a caret-width bar bracketing each end (iA's touch handles minus the iOS knobs) and a short tail for a selected line break. Blink is a 1.06 s soft fade that switches off on every keystroke and caret move and returns after 480 ms of quiet; short moves glide 62/92 ms, long jumps and fast typing snap; unfocused, the caret stays as a quiet ghost and the highlight goes neutral. Typing latency unchanged (p50 2.44 ms to present, 100% within one 60 Hz frame).
secondary: Both files are 1924x1240, same viewport; caret hex identical (#00B5FF) in both, so colour is not a differentiator.

A's caret edges are hard-cut (736 px = exactly 8x92, zero antialiased pixels); B's light caret has a few antialiased/lighter rows at the cap (#00C6FF) — a half-pixel difference, immaterial either way.
Caret height equals 100% of the 46 CSS px line box in both, i.e. ~9px of blue above the ascender — neither app trims the caret to ascender-plus-descender, which is why it reads heavy at rest.
Neither screenshot conveys blink or motion; the caret's aliveness is unjudgeable from these stills and both rely purely on width and saturation for presence.
B's selection fill (#003E4C) is marginally darker than A's (#143E4F) against the same #1A1A1A ground — a fine choice on its own, ruined by the dimmed glyphs sitting on it.
